articles.title: AI in Medical Imaging: What It Can and Cannot Do
articles.excerpt: Computer tools are being studied to help clinicians read scans. Here is a plain-language look at how they are used and why a clinician stays in charge.
articles.body: Researchers and hospitals are exploring software that highlights possible findings on images such as X-rays, skin photos and eye scans. These tools are generally designed to assist a trained clinician, not to replace one. Performance can differ between tools, patient groups and hospitals, and a tool that works well in one setting may not work as well in another. Software can also miss findings or flag things that turn out to be harmless. For this reason, results are reviewed by a qualified professional before any decision about care is made. If you have a health concern, speak to a doctor rather than relying on any app or tool.

articles.title: How mRNA Vaccines Work: A Plain-Language Explainer
articles.excerpt: A short overview of what an mRNA vaccine is and how it prompts the body to prepare its defences.
articles.body: An mRNA vaccine carries a short set of instructions that lets your cells make a harmless piece of a germ, such as a protein found on its surface. Your immune system recognises that piece as foreign and learns to respond to it, so it is better prepared if you meet the real germ later. The instructions break down naturally soon afterwards. Like all vaccines, these can cause short-lived side effects such as a sore arm or tiredness. Your doctor or local health authority can tell you which vaccines are recommended for you and when.

articles.title: Digital Mental-Health Apps: A Helpful Tool, Not a Replacement
articles.excerpt: Apps can support habits like mood tracking and breathing exercises, but they do not replace professional care.
articles.body: Many people use apps for mood tracking, guided breathing, meditation and sleep routines. These can be a useful addition to everyday self-care. They are not a substitute for a qualified mental-health professional, especially if you are struggling with persistent low mood, anxiety or thoughts of harming yourself. If you are in distress, contact someone you trust, a doctor, or a helpline. In India you can call Tele-MANAS on 14416 or, in an emergency, 112.

articles.title: Gut Health and the Brain: An Active Area of Research
articles.excerpt: Scientists are studying links between the digestive system and brain health. The science is still developing.
articles.body: The community of microbes in the gut is an area of active scientific interest, including how it may relate to mood, immunity and long-term health. Much of the work is early-stage, and findings in the laboratory or in animals do not always carry over to people. At present, general advice remains familiar: eat a varied diet with plenty of fibre, stay active and speak to a doctor before trying any treatment that claims to change your gut bacteria.

articles.title: Why Antiviral Research Is Difficult
articles.excerpt: Viruses change quickly and use our own cells to multiply, which makes safe treatments hard to design.
articles.body: Viruses depend on the cells they infect, so a medicine that stops a virus must avoid harming healthy cells. Many viruses also mutate, and a treatment that works against one strain may work less well against another. This is one reason prevention, such as vaccination, good hygiene and staying home when unwell, plays an important role alongside treatment. If you think you have a serious infection, seek medical care.

articles.title: Smart Wound Dressings: Research Directions
articles.excerpt: Researchers are exploring dressings with sensors that could help monitor wounds. Most are not yet in everyday use.
articles.body: Ideas under investigation include dressings that can sense changes such as temperature or moisture to help clinicians monitor healing. Such technologies are largely at the research or early-testing stage. For everyday wound care, standard guidance still applies: keep the wound clean, cover it, watch for redness, swelling, pus or fever, and see a doctor if you notice signs of infection or the wound is deep.

articles.title: Why Consistent Sleep Matters for Health
articles.excerpt: Regular, sufficient sleep supports mood, memory, immunity and heart health.
articles.body: Sleep is when the body and brain do important maintenance. Health organisations generally advise that most adults aim for seven or more hours a night. Keeping regular sleep and wake times, limiting caffeine late in the day, reducing screens before bed and keeping the bedroom dark and cool can help. If you have persistent trouble sleeping, loud snoring with pauses in breathing, or daytime sleepiness that affects your safety, talk to a doctor.

articles.title: Why Flu Vaccines Are Updated Every Year
articles.excerpt: Influenza viruses change from season to season, so the vaccine is reviewed regularly.
articles.body: Influenza viruses change over time, so health agencies review which strains are circulating and update seasonal flu vaccines accordingly. Protection from a vaccine can also fade, which is another reason yearly vaccination is commonly recommended for many people. Whether and when you should be vaccinated depends on your age and health, so ask your doctor or local health authority.
